findings.title: Both repeat items went to zero LSV in current week after sustained 4-week problem
findings.claim: The two items flagged as repeat alerts (KINGSIZE STANDARD item 769679 and SUPERKINGS STANDARD item 702015) both recorded £0 LSV in the current week (June 8-14), following four consecutive weeks of availability problems totaling £916 and £378 respectively. Daily data confirms item 769679 had no LSV since June 5 and item 702015 had no LSV since May 30, suggesting the chronic availability problem has been resolved. However, actual sales volume data shows both items continue selling small quantities (6-11 units/day for 769679, 1-2 units/day for 702015), indicating stock is now on shelf.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing signal reports cumulative LSV over 4 weeks and flags these as REPEAT alerts, but does not indicate whether the problem is ongoing or resolved. This finding adds critical temporal context: the availability issue appears to have been fixed before the current week, which changes the action required from urgent intervention to monitoring for recurrence.

findings.title: Store 408 CIGARETTES LSV is 44% above chain average despite recent improvement
findings.claim: Over the 5-week period (May 11 - June 14), Store 408 recorded £5,512 total lost sales in CIGARETTES, which is 44% higher than the chain average of £3,826 per store. This places Store 408 among the worst performers chain-wide for cigarette availability. The department-wide problem extends beyond the two repeat alert items: in the current week alone (when those two items showed £0 LSV), five other cigarette items accounted for £213 in lost sales, led by item 546 at £74.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing signal provides item-level detail for the two repeat alerts but does not contextualize Store 408's overall CIGARETTES department performance vs. the chain. This finding reveals the store has a broader department-level availability problem (44% worse than chain), not just isolated to two SKUs, which suggests systemic issues with cigarette category replenishment or ordering.

findings.title: KINGSIZE STANDARD item 769679 LSV concentrated on Thursdays (37% of weekly total)
findings.claim: For item 769679 (KINGSIZE STANDARD), lost sales over the 5-week period showed a strong Thursday concentration, with £295 LSV on Thursdays compared to £46-£152 on other days. Thursday accounts for 37% of total weekly LSV for this item. This pattern suggests a replenishment timing issue, where stock runs out mid-to-late week. The item had zero actual sales on all days with high LSV (May 15-23), confirming complete stockouts rather than low availability.
findings.novelty_rationale: The existing signal does not break down LSV by day of week or identify replenishment timing patterns. This finding adds actionable detail: the Thursday spike points to a specific delivery or ordering cycle problem that the store manager can address by reviewing mid-week replenishment schedules for this high-value cigarette SKU.

iterations.notes: Item 769679 (KINGSIZE STANDARD) does not appear in the top 5 current-week LSV items because it had £0 LSV in the current week, having resolved by June 5. The broader department problem (44% above chain) persists even with the two repeat items now available, indicating Store 408 needs a systematic review of cigarette ordering/replenishment processes.

findings.title: Problem has shifted to KINGSIZE MILD/LIGHTS with £190 LSV this week, double the chain average
findings.claim: While the two original repeat-alert items (KINGSIZE STANDARD and SUPERKINGS STANDARD) resolved, Store 408's cigarette availability problem has shifted to KINGSIZE MILD/LIGHTS, which recorded £190 LSV in the current week (June 8-14). This is 105% above the chain average of £93 per store for this PPG, and represents 59% of Store 408's total cigarette LSV this week. Chain-wide, KINGSIZE MILD/LIGHTS ranks 2nd in LSV (£11.4k total), but at Store 408 it is now the worst-performing PPG, having sustained elevated LSV for 5 consecutive weeks (£440, £313, £110, £251, £190 by week). The original repeat-alert PPGs (KINGSIZE STANDARD and SUPERKINGS STANDARD) are now showing minimal LSV (£18 and £42 respectively this week), confirming the problem has migrated rather than resolved.
findings.novelty_rationale: Prior findings established that the two repeat items resolved and that Store 408 is 44% above chain overall. This finding is new because it identifies *where* the problem has shifted to—a specific PPG category (KINGSIZE MILD/LIGHTS) that was not mentioned in the repeat alert or prior findings. It quantifies Store 408's disadvantage in this specific PPG (105% above chain) and shows sustained multi-week elevation, indicating a systematic ordering/replenishment issue has migrated to a different cigarette category.

findings.title: Item 546 (KINGSIZE MILD/LIGHTS) shows intermittent stockouts with £74 LSV spike in current week
findings.claim: Item 546, a KINGSIZE MILD/LIGHTS cigarette, is the single largest driver of current-week LSV at Store 408 with £74 lost sales (23% of total cigarette LSV this week). This item shows an intermittent stockout pattern across the 5-week period: £27 LSV in week of May 12, £26 in week of May 19, zero LSV for two weeks (May 26 and June 2), then a sharp spike to £74 in the current week (June 9-14). Day-of-week analysis reveals stockouts concentrate on Thursdays (£42 LSV) and Tuesdays (£40), with minimal weekend impact. Despite the spike, the item sold only 2 units total in the current week, suggesting near-complete stockout for most of the week. This contrasts with the resolved repeat items which had sustained multi-week outages; item 546 appears to have inconsistent ordering rather than chronic unavailability.
findings.novelty_rationale: Prior findings focused on the two repeat-alert items (769679 and 702015) and noted 'five other cigarette items' drove current-week LSV but did not drill into specifics. This finding identifies the #1 current-week item by name, quantifies its contribution (23% of total), reveals its intermittent pattern (vs the chronic pattern of repeat items), and identifies specific weekdays (Tue/Thu) where stockouts occur. This is actionable: the store can review Tuesday/Thursday ordering processes for this specific high-value item.

findings.title: Second MILD/LIGHTS item (32958) shows alternating bi-weekly stockout pattern with £60 current-week LSV
findings.claim: Item 32958, also in KINGSIZE MILD/LIGHTS, is the second-largest driver of current-week LSV at £60 (19% of total cigarette LSV). This item exhibits a distinct bi-weekly alternating pattern: £137 LSV in week of May 12, zero for two weeks, £146 in week of June 2, then £44 in the current week. The item sold 5 units in the current week despite £60 LSV, indicating partial availability. Together, items 546 and 32958 account for £134 of the £190 KINGSIZE MILD/LIGHTS LSV (71%), confirming that two specific SKUs within this PPG are responsible for Store 408's new problem. The bi-weekly pattern suggests possible confusion over reorder cycles or competing with the previously problematic STANDARD cigarettes for ordering attention.
findings.novelty_rationale: This extends the prior finding about item 546 by identifying the #2 item in the new problem PPG and revealing a *different* temporal pattern (bi-weekly alternation vs intermittent spikes). Together these two items explain 71% of the KINGSIZE MILD/LIGHTS problem. This is new and actionable: the store now knows exactly which two MILD/LIGHTS cigarettes need ordering process fixes, and the different patterns (weekly intermittent vs bi-weekly cycle) suggest different root causes that may require separate interventions.

iterations.notes: All three findings focus on the KINGSIZE MILD/LIGHTS PPG because this is where the problem has clearly shifted after the two repeat items (KINGSIZE STANDARD and SUPERKINGS STANDARD) resolved. The daily timeseries shows Store 408's total cigarette LSV remains elevated (though lower than May peaks), confirming the department-wide issue persists. Items 546 and 32958 together account for £134 of the £190 KINGSIZE MILD/LIGHTS LSV, so identifying these two specific items provides clear actionability. The different temporal patterns (intermittent weekly spikes vs bi-weekly alternation) suggest different root causes that may help the store manager diagnose whether the issue is ordering frequency, reorder quantity, or supplier delivery timing.

iterations.notes:
After 14 tool calls, I found a significant new angle that prior iterations missed: SUPERKINGS MILD/LIGHTS showed a dramatic spike pattern peaking at £482 LSV in week of May 19, then declining sharply to £59 in current week. This PPG was overlooked by prior iterations which focused entirely on KINGSIZE variants.

However, on closer examination this does NOT clear the novelty bar because:

1. The SUPERKINGS MILD/LIGHTS elevated LSV (£1,311 over 5 weeks, 116% above chain average) is broadly similar to the KINGSIZE MILD/LIGHTS finding from Iteration 2, just in a different PPG. The pattern (spike then resolution) is not meaningfully different.

2. Three items (14181, 747157, 32957) in SUPERKINGS MILD/LIGHTS show the same resolution behavior as the original repeat items: sustained LSV through late May, then complete resolution (£0 LSV) in current week. This is the same pattern already documented in Iteration 1 for items 769679 and 702015.

3. The day-of-week pattern for SUPERKINGS MILD/LIGHTS shows fairly even distribution across weekdays (Sun-Mon highest at £222-£213, with Sat lowest at £142), which is different from the Thursday spike documented for KINGSIZE STANDARD in Iteration 1, but this is not actionable as the problem has already resolved.

4. Item 32958 (KINGSIZE MILD/LIGHTS) shows partial resolution - LSV dropped from £60 in last week to £0 in current week (June 11-14), confirming the bi-weekly pattern from Iteration 2 has shifted but again this is just tracking an already-documented item's evolution.

The core insight - that Store 408 systematically resolved availability issues across multiple PPGs in late May/early June, with problems shifting between related cigarette categories - is already captured by Iterations 1 and 2's findings. Current week shows only £77 SUPERKINGS MILD/LIGHTS LSV from 3 items (794150, 32957, 794153), which represents normal operational variation rather than a chronic pattern worth flagging.

I considered exploring whether the resolution of KINGSIZE items caused SUPERKINGS items to spike (capacity constraint hypothesis), but the timeseries shows SUPERKINGS MILD/LIGHTS actually peaked in week of May 19 while KINGSIZE STANDARD was still elevated, contradicting a simple substitution theory.

No findings meet the novelty threshold given prior iterations' comprehensive coverage.

hypotheses_explored: 1. Does Store 408 have unusually low cigarette sales volume compared to chain, suggesting the LSV problem is masking an underlying demand issue (e.g., demographic mismatch, competition)?

2. Despite high LSV, is Store 408 actually selling MORE cigarettes than typical stores when available, indicating the LSV problem is driven by under-ordering for high demand rather than poor availability management?
3. Has the dramatic LSV decline from May 17 peak (£510/day) to current week (£12-£78/day) been matched by actual sales volume changes, or has demand remained constant while availability improved?
iterations.notes:
After 12 tool calls exploring a completely different angle than prior iterations (sales volume vs LSV relationship, rather than item/PPG-level LSV patterns), I found that Store 408 is NOT underperforming in cigarette sales despite the high LSV:

- Store 408 sold 1,680 units over 5 weeks (May 11 - June 14), which is 19% ABOVE the chain average of 1,414 units per store. This places Store 408 in the upper half of cigarette sales volume chain-wide (NOT in the bottom 10, which ranged from 221-753 units).

- The top 10 cigarette-selling stores averaged 2,500+ units, so Store 408 is mid-tier but definitely not a low-demand store.

- Store 408's high LSV (£5,512, 44% above chain as documented in Iteration 1) combined with above-average actual sales volume (19% above chain) suggests the problem is under-ordering for demand rather than poor availability management in a low-demand context.

However, this does NOT clear the novelty bar because:

1. The "under-ordering for demand" interpretation is already implicit in Iteration 1's finding that Store 408 LSV is 44% above chain. The new angle (19% above-chain sales volume) adds context but doesn't change the actionability.

2. The daily LSV timeseries shows a clear decline from peak of £510 on May 17 to £12-£78 in current week (June 8-14), which matches the resolution pattern already documented in Iterations 1-3. The actual sales volume remained relatively stable across weeks (307-354 units/week, with current week at 307), confirming availability improved while demand stayed constant - but again, this is already captured by prior findings about item-level resolutions.

3. Item 769679 (the primary repeat alert item) showed actual sales volume increasing from 4 units in week of May 5 to 45 units in current week, which directly confirms the resolution story from Iteration 1 (£0 LSV in current week because stock is now available). This is supportive evidence for an existing finding, not a new finding.

4. I considered whether Store 408's 19% above-chain sales volume combined with being in the mid-tier (not bottom 10) might indicate a store format or demographic mismatch that drives higher cigarette demand, but without store hierarchy data showing format differences this would be speculation.

The core insight - that Store 408 has above-average cigarette demand which was poorly served by under-ordering in May, leading to high LSV, but has since been resolved - is essentially a restatement of what Iterations 1-3 already documented from the item/PPG level.

No findings meet the novelty threshold. Prior iterations have comprehensively covered this signal from multiple angles (item-level resolution, PPG migration, day-of-week patterns, chain comparison). The sales volume angle confirms but does not extend their conclusions.

Prior iterations focused exclusively on cigarette PPGs (KINGSIZE/SUPERKINGS variants) without exploring tobacco despite it being larger by LSV.

2. Are there items in HAND ROLLING TOBACCO showing the same May spike + early June resolution pattern as the cigarette items, suggesting a systemic ordering/replenishment fix across the entire tobacco category?
3. Does Store 408 have unusually high markdown or wastage activity in cigarettes or related categories during the 5-week period that might explain or correlate with the availability issues?
iterations.notes:
After 14 tool calls exploring three distinct angles that prior iterations did not investigate, I found significant patterns but none that clear the novelty threshold:

**HAND ROLLING TOBACCO angle (calls 7-13):**
Store 408 recorded £4,028 LSV in HAND ROLLING TOBACCO over 5 weeks, which is 73% above chain average (£2,335 per store). This PPG is actually the largest LSV driver chain-wide (£286k total, vs £220k for KINGSIZE STANDARD) and the single largest at Store 408 (£4,028 vs £2,170 for KINGSIZE STANDARD). However:
- The temporal pattern shows the EXACT same May spike + June resolution as cigarettes: £1,231 LSV week of May 12, peak of £1,727 week of May 19, declining to £754/£213 in late May/early June, then only £38 in current week (June 8-14).
- Top item 13525 (£738 total LSV) had complete stockout May 15-23, then £0 LSV from May 24 onward — identical resolution pattern to the repeat cigarette items documented in Iteration 1.
- Current week shows minimal LSV (£45 from item 24057, £11 from item 178702), confirming resolution.

This is essentially the same finding as Iterations 1-3 but in a different product category. The novelty would be "Store 408's May availability crisis extended beyond cigarettes to tobacco," but this doesn't add actionable value since the problem has already resolved by current week across all categories.

**Markdown/Wastage angle (calls 1-6):**
Store 408 marked down 5,968 units and wasted 1,560 units over 5 weeks. However:
- Top markdown items are fresh/chilled (item 5000128271165 with 172 units, item 5000128966429 with 158) which are NOT related to cigarettes/tobacco.
- Top wastage items are fresh produce (item 540390 "CP SWEET PEPPER PACK" with 529 units, item 9836462 "BANANA F/T SNACKING" with 197), again unrelated to the cigarette/tobacco OSA signal.
- There is no evidence of correlation between the cigarette availability problems and markdown/wastage activity. This suggests the cigarette issue was pure under-ordering rather than over-ordering leading to waste.

This confirms the "under-ordering for demand" interpretation from Iteration 4 but doesn't add new actionability.

**Why no findings:**
All three angles explored either:
1) Confirm patterns already documented (May spike + June resolution now extends to HAND ROLLING TOBACCO)
2) Provide supportive evidence for existing conclusions (no waste correlation supports under-ordering theory)
3) Show negative results (markdown/wastage unrelated to the signal)

Prior iterations comprehensively documented the cigarette availability crisis and its resolution. The HAND ROLLING TOBACCO pattern is notable but represents the same systemic issue in a parallel category rather than a distinct finding. The store manager's action (improve ordering processes for tobacco products) was already implicit in prior findings about cigarettes.

Given 4 prior iterations covering item-level resolution, PPG migration, sales volume analysis, and day-of-week patterns, plus this iteration's exploration of parallel categories and waste correlation, the signal has been thoroughly investigated.
